title: New DNS RR Definitions
summary: Defines five new DNS resource record types for experimental use, covering things such as the location of AFS database servers, a responsible person for a domain, X.25 and ISDN addresses, and route-through information. It is an Experimental RFC that invited discussion and feedback rather than a standard.

eli5.summary: The phone book for the Internet learns a few new kinds of entries, like who to contact for a name. These are tried out as a test first.

subtitle: Five experimental DNS record types: AFS server locations, a responsible person, X.25 and ISDN addresses, and route-through bindings.

tldr.problem: DNS had no standard way to say where AFS database servers are, who is responsible for a host, or what the X.25 or ISDN address of a host is.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five new resource record types, AFSDB, RP, X25, ISDN and RT, with their formats, type codes and examples, and marks all of them experimental.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental RFC that asks the community for discussion and suggestions. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and has itself been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 1183 is an Experimental RFC from October 1990. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and has itself been updated by RFC 5395, RFC 5864, RFC 6195 and RFC 6895.

sections.title: Five New Record Types
sections.content:
RFC 1183 defines the format of new resource records (RRs) for the Domain Name System and reserves matching type mnemonics and numeric codes. It has three independent parts: locating AFS database servers, locating responsible persons, and representing X.25 and ISDN addresses along with route binding. All of it is experimental.

The memo assumes the reader already knows DNS from RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and says its data is for teaching and does not necessarily reflect the real Internet.
sections.eli5: This document adds five new kinds of lines to the Internet's phone book. Each one answers a question that the old phone book could not.

sections.title: AFSDB: Locating AFS and DCE Servers
sections.content:
The AFSDB record (type code 18) maps a domain name to the host that runs a database server for an AFS cell or for an OSF DCE cell. Its format is <owner> <ttl> <class> AFSDB <subtype> <hostname>. Both data fields are required, the subtype is a 16 bit integer, and the hostname names a host with a server for the cell named by the owner.

Subtype 1 means the host has an AFS version 3.0 Volume Location Server for the cell. Subtype 2 means it has an authenticated name server holding the cell-root directory node for a DCE/NCA cell. The record triggers address (type A) additional section processing for the hostname. That is the stated reason for a new type instead of using TXT records. In a master file it looks the same as MX.
sections.eli5: If you want to find the library that holds a certain set of files, this entry points you to the computer that knows where the shelves are.

sections.title: RP: The Responsible Person
sections.content:
Often it is hard to find who to contact when a host is down. Mail to POSTMASTER may not reach the right person, and the zone contact in the SOA record is about the zone database. The RP record (type code 17) lets any name in the DNS point to a responsible person.

It has two required fields: <mbox-dname>, a domain name that encodes the person's mailbox the same way the SOA RNAME field does, and <txt-dname>, a domain name at which TXT records hold free-form text for humans. The root name . in either field means no mailbox or no TXT record. The extra level of indirection lets many hosts point at the same TXT description.

An RP record can sit on any node of the tree, not only at the leaves. A name may have several RP records, and they should have identical TTLs. RP records cause no additional section processing.
sections.eli5: This entry says: if this computer breaks, call this person. A second part points to a note with the person's details, so many computers can share one note.

sections.title: X25, ISDN and RT: Addresses and Route Binding
sections.content:
The third part is an experimental way to store wide area network addresses in DNS. The X25 record (type code 19) holds a Public Switched Data Network address in the X.121 numbering plan, as a string of decimal digits starting with the 4 digit DNIC. National prefixes such as a 0 must not be used. The ISDN record (type code 20) holds an ISDN number, which is a telephone number following E.163 and E.164, plus an optional subaddress written as hexadecimal digits.

The RT record (type code 21) is a route-through binding for hosts without their own direct wide area address. It has a 16 bit preference, where smaller is more preferred, and the name of an intermediate host that should have at least one A, X25 or ISDN record. It works much like MX. A host looks for RT records for its destination, drops any with a preference higher than or equal to its own if it appears in the set, and falls back to the destination's own address records if none remain. RT records do not chain.

The RFC names several possible uses, all experimental: documenting addresses for static IP over X.25 and SMTP over X.25 setups, automatic use by a network-layer router, and a proposal for a next-generation internet.
sections.eli5: These entries store phone-style numbers for some older kinds of networks. The route entry says: to reach this computer, go through that one first.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not addressed in this memo. The record types are published for experiment and carry no authentication or protection of their own in this document.
sections.eli5: The authors did not talk about safety at all in this document. It was just an experiment.
